comparison: Both strongly support the achievement of >90% editing efficiency through protocol modifications (C1-C3, C37, C40-C42). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and dose-response relationships, while peer reviewers highlight this as a 'major advance' with 'convincing' evidence. Peer review also includes DNA-PK inhibitor claims (C32, C34-C35, C56) in their evaluation.

Both support the DNA-PK inhibitor optimization claims (C32, C34-C35, C56). OpenEval treats this as a separate finding with focus on AZD7648's optimal performance, while peer reviewers group it with overall efficiency achievements as part of the major methodological advance.

Perfect agreement on claims C4, C45, C61, C107 regarding even editing across HSPC hierarchy. Both acknowledge the lack of in vivo transplantation data as a limitation. Peer reviewers specifically highlight this as a unique contribution 'beyond what was done in the other manuscript.'

Both support the finding of modest decrease in advanced progenitors (C5, C46). OpenEval includes C94 connecting this to CFC frequency, while peer review includes C61 (hierarchy preservation). Both characterize the effect as not substantially distorting the hierarchy.

Both support preserved differentiation capacity in CFC assays (C6, C49, C62). OpenEval emphasizes equivalent colony type proportions despite decreased total numbers. Peer reviewers include C74 and describe evidence as 'convincing' that 'functional progenitors can be successfully edited.'

Both support LTC-IC preservation claims (C7, C51). OpenEval includes C77 and emphasizes statistical analysis methodology. Peer reviewers include C107 and explicitly state evidence is 'convincing' that 'primitive LTC-ICs were minimally affected,' treating this as a key finding.

Perfect agreement on zygosity tuning capability (C8, C53, C55, C97, C108). Both treat this as an important methodological contribution. Peer reviewers explicitly state it was 'convincingly presented and provides a valuable strategy' for disease modeling.

Both support off-target safety findings (C43-C44, C67, C106). OpenEval notes the limitation to predicted sites without genome-wide assessment. Peer reviewers include C68 and explicitly state evidence is 'convincing' regarding 'lack of edits at predicted off-target sites.'

Perfect agreement on RNP optimization without enhancer (C24-C26, C80-C81). Both support the efficiency-toxicity tradeoff decision. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of overall methodological rigor without explicit challenge.

Perfect agreement on donor type and concentration optimization (C29-C30, C82-C84). Both support the conclusions about optimal concentrations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings, noting 'methods are clearly described and experiments appropriately powered.'

Perfect agreement on toxicity mechanism interpretation (C31, C65-C66). Both support the conclusion that toxicity is mediated by innate immune responses rather than RNP. OpenEval notes this remains an inference; peer reviewers accept without challenge.

Both support the correlation between handling time and efficiency (C38-C39, C59-C60). OpenEval includes C95 and notes R²=0.55 indicates substantial unexplained variance. Peer reviewers explicitly value this as 'useful insights into optimizing practicalities' for bench scientists.

Perfect agreement on differential toxicity effects (C47-C48, C64, C103). Both support the interpretation that late progenitors are more sensitive. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'preservation of a pool of targeted progenitors' despite quantitative decrease.

Both strongly support the spacer mutation breakthrough for ssODN efficiency (C57-C58, C90). OpenEval emphasizes the dramatic improvement (44% to 94%). Peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as 'a promising advance towards democratizing these editing strategies.'

Perfect agreement on the limitation regarding lack of in vivo transplantation data (C102). Both rate this as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes LTC-IC data suggests but doesn't definitively confirm functional preservation. Peer reviewers state 'it remains to be verified' but find LTC-IC results 'encouraging.'
